random-variables-s1.title: People in a car at a toll booth
random-variables-s1.text: A highway agency records the number of people in each car that passes a toll booth. Let X = the number of people in a randomly chosen car. The probability for 5 people (the most a car can hold here) is missing (invented data).

table.caption: Probability distribution of X, the number of people in a car

random-variables-s2.title: Goals scored by a soccer team
random-variables-s2.text: Let G = the number of goals a club soccer team scores in a randomly chosen game. The probability histogram shows its distribution, built from several seasons of results (invented data).

plot.label: Probability histogram of G, goals in a game: 0.25 for 0 goals, 0.35 for 1, 0.22 for 2, 0.12 for 3 and 0.06 for 4

items.q: What probability belongs in the blank, $P(X = 5)$?

why.correct: The probabilities of a distribution add to 1: $1 - (0.45 + 0.30 + 0.12 + 0.09) = 1 - 0.96 = 0.04$.

mistakes.why: That spreads the probability evenly over 5 values. The probabilities must add to 1, so the blank is 1 minus the others.
That is the sum of the other probabilities. The blank is what is left: 1 − 0.96.

items.q: What is the probability that a randomly chosen car has at least 3 people?

mistakes.why: That is $P(X = 3)$ only. At least 3 includes 4 and 5.

items.q: What is the probability that a car has fewer than 3 people?

mistakes.why: That is $P(X \le 3)$. "Fewer than 3" does not include 3.
That is the complement, 3 or more.

items.q: Which is a complete definition of the random variable in this context?

why.correct: A random variable is a number that comes from a chance process, defined in context: what is counted, and for which randomly chosen individual.
options: People are not a number. Say what is counted: the number of people.
Right: a count, in context, for one random car.
X takes values like 1 to 5; probabilities describe how likely each value is.
Cars are the individuals, not the numerical value being recorded.
X = the people in the cars at the toll booth
X = the number of people in a randomly chosen car at the toll booth
X = the probability that a car has more than one person
X = the cars that pass through the toll booth on a randomly chosen day

why.correct: A cumulative probability adds every value up to the boundary: $0.45 + 0.30 + 0.12 = 0.87$.

mistakes.why: That is $P(X = 3)$ alone; cumulative adds 1, 2 and 3.

items.q: Which describes the shape of the distribution of G?

why.correct: The tallest bar is at 1 and the bars trail off toward 3 and 4 goals: a longer tail to the right, so skewed right.
options: The long tail is toward the larger values, 3 and 4.
The bars are much lower on the right than on the left.
Uniform would need equal bar heights.
Right: the tail is on the high side.
Skewed left, with a peak at 1 goal and a tail toward 0 goals
Roughly symmetric, centered at 2 goals
Uniform, since each number of goals is possible
Skewed right, with a peak at 1 goal and a tail toward 4

items.q: What is the probability that the team scores at least 2 goals in a game?

mistakes.why: That is $P(G > 2)$, which leaves out 2 goals.

items.q: What kind of random variable is G?

why.correct: G takes a list of separate values (0, 1, 2, 3, 4), so it is a discrete random variable.
options: The variable is goals, not time.
Right: goals are counted.
G is a number from a chance process; the bars are its values.
It cannot be 2.5 goals; only whole numbers are possible.
Continuous, because a game lasts for 90 minutes of playing time
Discrete, because it takes separate whole-number values
Categorical, because each bar is a category
Continuous, because it can be any number from 0 to 4

items.q: The cumulative probability $P(G \le 1)$ is 0.60. What does it mean in context?

why.correct: $P(G \le 1) = 0.25 + 0.35 = 0.60$: in the long run, the team scores 1 goal or fewer in about 60% of its games.
options: That would be $P(G = 1)$, which is 0.35.
That is $P(G \ge 1) = 0.75$.
Right: a cumulative probability up to 1 goal.
A cumulative probability is a probability, not a number of goals.
In about 60% of games, the team scores exactly 1 goal
In about 60% of games, the team scores at least 1 goal
In about 60% of games, the team scores 1 goal or fewer
The team scores 0.60 goals in a typical game

why.correct: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of a chance process, such as the number of heads in 3 flips.
options: The randomness is in the outcome, not in choosing the variable.
A random variable takes numerical values.
A random variable varies from trial to trial.
Right: its values come with probabilities.
A variable that was chosen at random from a list of variables
Any categorical variable recorded in a survey
A number that stays the same from one trial of a chance process to the next
A numerical value that depends on the outcome of a chance process

items.q: Which table is a valid probability distribution for a random variable W that takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3?

why.correct: Each probability must be from 0 to 1 and the four must add to 1: $0.1 + 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1$.
options: Right: each between 0 and 1, sum 1.
These add to 1.1, more than 1.
A probability cannot be negative.
These add to 0.9, less than 1.

why.correct: A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, like a time measured as precisely as you like. Counts are discrete.
options: Texts are counted, so the variable is discrete.
Right: time can be any value in a range.
Heads are counted: 0 to 10.
Cars are counted.
The number of texts a randomly chosen student sends in a day
The time a randomly chosen runner takes to finish a mile
The number of heads in 10 flips of a coin
The number of red cars in a parking lot chosen at random

items.q: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. Let H = the number of heads. Find $P(H = 2)$.

why.correct: The 8 equally likely outcomes include HHT, HTH and THH with 2 heads: $P(H = 2) = \frac{3}{8} = 0.375$. The full distribution is 0.125, 0.375, 0.375, 0.125 for 0 to 3 heads.

mistakes.why: That treats the values 0, 1, 2 and 3 as equally likely. Count the 8 outcomes instead.
That counts one arrangement, HHT. There are 3 ways to get 2 heads.

items.q: Let W = the number of extended warranties a store sells in a randomly chosen hour, with $P(W = 0) = 0.50$, $P(W = 1) = 0.30$, $P(W = 2) = 0.15$ and $P(W = 3) = 0.05$. Write an expression for $P(W \ge 1)$ using the complement rule.

mistakes.why: That is $P(W = 1)$ only. At least 1 is 1, 2 or 3.
That leaves out $P(W = 1) = 0.30$. At least 1 means 1, 2 or 3, which is everything except 0.

items.q: A playlist of 12 songs is shuffled and a student counts the rock songs. Which definition of the random variable would earn full credit on the exam?

why.correct: Define the random variable as a number in context: what is counted and out of what. "Rock songs" names things, not a number.
options: Right: a count, with what is counted and out of how many.
That names things, not a number.
That is a probability, not the random count.
That is a categorical outcome, not a numerical random variable.
Let R = the number of rock songs among the 12 songs on the playlist
Let R = rock songs
Let R = the probability that a song is a rock song
Let R = whether each song on the shuffled playlist is rock or not rock

items.q: For a discrete random variable Y with whole-number values, $P(Y \le 2) = 0.80$ and $P(Y \le 1) = 0.55$. Find $P(Y = 2)$.

why.correct: Cumulative probabilities differ by the values between them: $P(Y = 2) = P(Y \le 2) - P(Y \le 1) = 0.80 - 0.55 = 0.25$.

mistakes.why: That is the cumulative probability up to 2, not the probability of exactly 2.
Adding cumulative probabilities double counts; subtract them.
